html:
Brussels became the main seat of the European institutions after the Treaty of Rome came into force in 1958. The Berlaymont building, finished in 1969, is the headquarters of the European Commission.

The six founding states could not agree on a capital, so the institutions spread across Brussels, Luxembourg and Strasbourg. Brussels gained the Commission and the Council of Ministers, and much of the work of the European Parliament. NATO moved its headquarters to Brussels in 1967 after France left its military command.

The European quarter, with its offices, lobbyists and diplomats, made Brussels one of the most international cities in the world. It shows how Belgium, itself a country of divided languages, became the working home of the European Union.
